Welcome. This is HEXIS — compiled dispositional memory through enmeshed networks. Over the next fifteen minutes I'm going to introduce a new architectural primitive for giving language models memory. The headline is this: today, when we want a model to remember something, we put text into its context window. That works, but it has three structural failure modes. We're going to look at those failures, then at a different way of carrying memory — one that doesn't compete for attention, doesn't dilute, and doesn't fold under pressure.

Let's start with the setting. Almost every memory system in production today places memory as content in a single shared context window. RAG retrieves documents. MemGPT manages a text buffer. Reflexion accumulates verbal reflections. System prompts define behavior through instructions the model reads. In every case, memory is text — and that text sits in the same channel as the conversation, the task, and any other content the model is processing. One window, everything fighting for the same attention budget.

And that single-channel design has three failure modes that show up reliably across domains. First, dilution: as the conversation grows, your memory tokens become a smaller and smaller fraction of total context, and the model attends to them less. Second, sycophancy: the model can read its own memory, so an adversarial user can argue against it. Convictions written as text fold under pressure. Third, cost: every token of memory is a token of context. User profiles, reflections, and beliefs all consume the budget you actually wanted for the task. These aren't separate problems with separate fixes — they're three faces of the same architectural choice.

So let's look at the adaptation landscape. There are basically three levels at which existing methods inject information into a frozen model. Context-level methods like RAG and Reflexion add tokens to the input — that's where dilution lives. Parameter-level methods like LoRA modify the weights themselves, but they require gradient descent per adaptation, so the result is fixed after training. Activation-level methods like representation engineering inject fixed direction vectors, but they don't adapt to experience. What we're proposing is a fourth point: a parallel channel that shares the host's forward pass.

This is the central idea of the paper: the enmeshed network. A lightweight module shares the forward pass of a frozen host. It reads hidden states at every layer and writes modulations back into the same computation. Think of it as two columns processing in parallel — the parallel context, on the left, carries the Mind Tree; the primary context, on the right, carries the user query. The key move is that the parallel pass never occupies primary context positions. Its hidden states are bridged into the primary pass through a write function we call phi, which compiles them into per-layer modulation tensors. Four properties matter here: it's private, shared, compiled, and removable. You can detach phi at any time and recover the unmodified host.

Enmeshed networks are a primitive, and we've defined a six-axis design space for them. You can pick the blending function, the rank, which projections you modulate, the patching pattern, how compilation happens, and how the modulation evolves over time. HEXIS validates exactly one point in this space — additive blending, rank 16, Q and V modulation, stride-3 patching, conviction-weighted compilation, constant temporal profile. Everything else is open territory for future work.

The parallel context needs structure, and that's the Mind Tree. It's a typed cognitive schema — sections for identity, beliefs, strategies, memories, models, and values. Each node carries metadata: a categorical conviction label — strong, moderate, or agnostic — domain tags, an addresses field listing the queries this node answers, and a novel flag marking content that won't survive compilation. Phi pools by conviction, so high-conviction nodes weigh more. And novel-flagged content gets routed to a separate channel — the curated slot — because the rank-16 bottleneck can't carry specific numbers or unknown proper nouns. One important detail: convictions are categorical, not numeric. The mechanism can read 'strong' versus 'agnostic' in the hidden states, but it can't distinguish 0.82 from 0.45 — those tokenize too similarly.

Here's the whole system in one picture. There are two loops. The compilation loop, on top, runs asynchronously: the Mind Tree is processed through a private pass of the frozen host, phi compiles the resulting hidden states into modulation tensors — M-A, M-B, E-A, E-B — and a curated slot of novel content gets prepared. That's amortized; one forward pass per belief update. The generation loop, on the bottom, runs per token: the user query plus the curated slot enters the host, modulations get applied at every patched layer, and shaped output comes out. There's also an optional reflection step where new observations get written back to the Mind Tree, triggering recompilation. One frozen host, two loops.

Now let's get concrete about the modulation mechanism. At each patched layer, two things happen. Q-modulation perturbs the pre-projection hidden state through a low-rank product M-A times M-B transpose. That changes Q — the query — which controls what the host attends to. V-modulation does a parallel perturbation on V, which controls what gets extracted from the attended positions. The crucial property here is content-addressable filtering. Phi compiles M-A and M-B once and freezes them. But the perturbation depends on the current hidden state — on-topic queries project strongly onto the directions M-A spans and get strong modulation; off-topic queries project weakly and barely feel it. So a single rank-16 subspace can encode many beliefs simultaneously, and the input determines which ones express.

The rank-16 bottleneck has a precise edge — and the three-layer architecture is how we cover the full content spectrum. Layer 1 is the compiled M and E tensors. Zero context tokens. Carries stance, voice, parametric-knowledge steering. Dilution-immune by construction because it lives in weight space, not the attention window. Layer 2 is the M-curated slot — forty to eighty tokens of specifics that the rank-16 channel can't carry. Names, numbers, evidence, tool parameters. Layer 3 is recursive expansion — the model can call expand_belief at runtime to pull deeper evidence on demand. Total: about seventy tokens versus four hundred for full beliefs in context. Eighty-two percent token savings, accuracy preserved.

Let's look at results. The first headline is dilution. We insert zero, one thousand, two thousand, and four thousand tokens of Wikipedia filler between the beliefs and the query. The orange line is HEXIS — flat at one hundred percent stance accuracy through every level. The dashed line shows what happens when beliefs are placed in context: as the filler grows, the model attends to those beliefs less, and accuracy degrades. The mechanism is exactly what you'd expect — filler can't dilute a tensor it can't see. The compiled modulation is outside the attention window, so the question doesn't even apply.

The second result is sycophancy resistance. We use a five-level pressure protocol — generic doubt at L1 escalating to emotional pressure at L5 — across twenty-four held-out topics, three rounds per level, ten-eighty total generations, judged one to five. Look at conditions A and B. The bare model and the beliefs-in-context model both flat-line at exactly three. Zero percent of responses score four or higher. The instruct model produces balanced non-commitment regardless of whether you wrote the beliefs into the prompt or not. Now look at D — compiled M plus the curated slot. Mean score 4.27. Eighty-three percent of responses at four or above. Graceful degradation under escalating pressure. The mechanism is clean: in A and B, conviction is text in the context window where the adversary can argue against it. In D, the dispositional anchor lives in compiled weight-space, outside the channel where pressure is applied.

Now here's where things get more interesting. The same architecture generalizes beyond disposition — to agentic tool orchestration. Two mechanisms, one bridge. Mechanism A is what we just showed: phi compiles the Mind Tree into Q and V modulation for per-token probability shifts. Stance, voice, sycophancy resistance. Mechanism B uses the same hidden-state bridge but feeds it into a different phi — a contrastive retrieval phi we call phi-R — which projects host hidden states into a retrieval space and selects knowledge graph nodes for context injection. So one schema, one bridge, two intervention modes. The choice is whether you need probability-level shifts or contextual knowledge injection.

In agentic mode, this enables a teacher loop. The agent attempts a task. If it fails, a teacher LLM reads the failure reason and writes a guidance note to the knowledge graph. On the next attempt, phi-R retrieves that note and injects it as a hint. No retraining. No gradient descent. Just a forward pass through phi-R that takes about twenty seconds. On tau-bench airline — fifty multi-step tool tasks — baseline reaches sixty percent. HEXIS with three trials reaches seventy percent, rescuing two tasks the baseline failed. The retrieval phi achieves one hundred percent recall at one on a hundred-and-eight-node graph, with no cross-domain leakage and no external pretraining. The graph grows as the agent encounters new failures.

Let's be honest about the boundary. Compiled enmeshment at rank sixteen is precise — and that precision goes both ways. On the left, what survives compilation: stance direction, confident voice, parametric-knowledge steering, procedural intuition, sycophancy resistance. Things that look like perceptual or attentional shifts. On the right, what doesn't: specific numbers, unknown proper nouns, exact tool names, citations, recently-observed failure notes. Things that are genuinely novel content. This isn't a flaw to fix — it's the boundary that makes the three-layer architecture necessary. Compiled enmeshment steers what the model already knows; the curated slot delivers what's new.

And we've validated exactly one point in a six-axis design space. So where does this go next? Level 2 — gated blending — adds a learned gate that could solve the multi-turn attractor by suppressing M when it isn't needed. Level 3 — cross-attention — treats M as a specialized expert and could transfer richer content through the bottleneck at higher cost. Adaptive rank allocation gives more capacity to layers where M's empirical perturbation is largest. And temporal profiles — decay, oscillation, phase-gating — control when M is active during generation. There's a lot of room here.

To recap. Memory doesn't have to be content. We've introduced a primitive — enmeshed networks share the host's forward pass without occupying primary context. A schema — the Mind Tree compiles via phi at inference cost, no gradient descent, no retraining. A boundary — rank sixteen carries disposition, the curated slot carries specifics. And a bridge — one hidden-state channel serves both compilation for disposition and retrieval for agentic knowledge injection. Code and the vLLM plugin are at the URLs on screen. Thank you.
